questions.question: Describe Tswana society on the southern borders of the Tswana world around 1800.
questions.expected_answer: Sotho-Tswana-speaking farmers in present-day North West, Northern Cape (Kuruman), south-eastern Botswana and parts of the Free State and Limpopo; chiefdoms led by a kgosi with advisers and the kgotla assembly (Bahurutshe, Bakwena, Bangwaketse, Barolong, Batlhaping); large dense towns divided into wards (Dithakong about 10-15 000 people in 1801, Kaditshwene, Molokwane) near water and for defence; women farmed sorghum, beans, melons, pumpkins; young men at distant cattle posts.

questions.question: What goods did the Tswana produce and trade?
questions.expected_answer: Hunting products: ivory, hides, skins, furs, ostrich feathers and eggshells (with San hunters); karosses - finely sewn fur cloaks; iron goods (hoes, axes, spearheads, knives, needles) from smelted ore; copper beads, bracelets, earrings and wire; pottery, woodcarving, baskets, medicines; sebilo (specularite powder from near Postmasburg). Traded these with the Kora and Griqua for glass beads, tobacco, cloth, wire, buttons, pots, later guns, gunpowder, horses, pack oxen and wagons.

questions.question: Explain how trade and contact changed the southern Tswana world.
questions.expected_answer: New goods and wealth for chiefs who controlled trade (e.g. Mothibi at Dithakong); Tswana as skilful traders and middlemen to the north; guns and horses changed warfare and hunting, causing a sharp decline in elephants; LMS mission among the Batlhaping (1816, Kuruman 1824) brought literacy, Christianity and irrigation but challenged customs and chiefs; insecurity from raids (Dithakong 1823), Kora/Griqua raiding, Ndebele and Boer movements; later loss of land - British Bechuanaland (1885), part of the Cape in 1895.
